A DAG is a durable record of a computation. Create one first, then add work to
it. Until `commit()`, `dag` is the live computation we are building.

```{python}
import daggerml as dml
from daggerml.contrib.funks import docker_build

dag = dml.new("docs-image", message="build the tutorial image")
```

## Put values in the DAG

`dag.put()` records a value and returns its node. Naming important nodes makes
them easy to find later without changing their identity.

```{python}
count = dag.put(3, name="count")
labels = dag.put(["fresh", "local", "seasonal"], name="labels")

print(count.value())
print(labels.value())
```

The values look like ordinary Python values when materialized with `.value()`,
but `count` and `labels` are nodes. They retain where they live in the DAG and
can be used as inputs without discarding that provenance.

## Access collections

Indexing a collection node creates another node. This matters when a downstream
result uses only part of a large or structured input: the graph records which
part was selected.

```{python}
first_label = labels[0]

print(first_label.value())
print(first_label.ref)
```

Dictionary access works the same way, including nested access.

```{python}
settings = dag.put(
    {"mode": "local", "limits": {"retries": 2}},
    name="settings",
)
mode = settings["mode"]
retries = settings["limits"]["retries"]

print(mode.value())
print(retries.value())
```

Nodes can be placed inside new collections. DaggerML records those
relationships; it does not replace the nodes with unrelated copies of their
Python values.

```{python}
summary = dag.put(
    {
        "count": count,
        "first_label": first_label,
        "mode": mode,
        "retries": retries,
    },
    name="summary",
)

print(summary.value())
print(dag.keys())
```

## Call a node

Functions are data in DaggerML. Putting `docker_build` in the DAG produces a
callable node; calling that node records both the inputs and the produced image.
For this live build, the harness quietly packages the current checkout into the
same S3-backed context used by this tutorial's Docker build.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import os
from pathlib import Path

from daggerml.contrib.s3 import S3Store

context_uri = S3Store().tar(
    str(Path(os.environ["DOCS_BUILD_ROOT"])),
    excludes=(
        ".git", ".dml", ".tools", "ignore", ".venv", ".mypy_cache",
        ".pytest_cache", "__pycache__", "*.pyc", "tests", "build", "dist",
        "dashboard-ui", "openspec", ".github",
        "src/daggerml/dashboard/static",
    ),
    symlinks="ignore",
)
```

```{python}
context = dag.put(context_uri, name="context-tarball")
build = dag.put(docker_build, name="build-image")
image = build(
    context,
    ["-f", "./docs/Dockerfile"],
    name="image",
)

print(image.value().uri.startswith("s3://"))
```

`image` is the result we want another DAG to reuse, so we commit it last. A
commit closes the live DAG and makes its named nodes, result, and provenance
durable.

```{python}
dag.commit(image)
```

The [Funks](funks.qmd) lesson now can import this exact result with
`dag.require()` and run code inside the image.
